query_text: Tell me about some weird habits that some people have.

parts.text:
Human beings are wonderfully complex, and we all have our own little rituals and quirks that help us navigate the world. What seems completely logical to one person might look utterly bizarre to another. 

Here are some of the most common "weird" habits that people have, categorized by how they manifest:

### 1. The Odd Food Ritualists
For some, eating isn't just about nutrition; it’s a highly structured performance.
* **The "One at a Time" Eater (Mono-eating):** Some people cannot eat their meals in a mixed fashion. They must eat all of one item on their plate before moving on to the next. For example, they will eat every single pea, then all the mashed potatoes, and finally the chicken—never mixing a bite.
* **The "No-Touch" Policy:** Many adults still suffer from *brumotactillophobia*—the fear of different foods touching on a plate. If the gravy from the mashed potatoes breaches the border of the green beans, the meal is compromised.
* **Food Deconstruction:** Some people can’t just eat food; they have to dismantle it. They will peel the chocolate coating off a Milky Way before eating the nougat, separate the layers of a wafer cookie, or peel the skin off grapes before eating them.
* **Smelling Every Bite:** Some people have an unconscious habit of smelling every single forkful of food right before they put it in their mouth, even if they've eaten that exact meal a hundred times.

### 2. Physical & Sensory Quirks
Many habits are born from how our bodies interact with the environment.
* **The "One-Foot-Out" Thermostat:** Millions of people cannot sleep without sticking exactly one foot out of the heavy blankets. Scientifically, this actually makes sense: our feet contain specialized blood vessels that help dissipate heat, making the foot act like a personal radiator to regulate body temperature.
* **Symmetry Obsession:** If some people accidentally stub their left toe or bump their right elbow against a wall, they feel a deep, nagging urge to mimic the sensation on the opposite side of their body to "even things out."
* **Step-Counting and Tile-Stepping:** Walking down a hallway or sidewalk becomes a game. Many people find themselves carefully stepping only within the boundaries of floor tiles, avoiding cracks on the sidewalk (the classic "step on a crack, break your mother's back"), or counting their steps in sets of four or eight.
* **Smelling Weird Things:** There is a large subset of the population obsessed with sniffing non-traditional scents. This includes the smell of new books (which actually has a name: *bibliosmia*), gasoline, Sharpie markers, rubbing alcohol, or the damp air of an old basement.

### 3. Cognitive & Verbal Habits
Sometimes our brains need external "hacks" to process information, resulting in quirky behaviors.
* **Narrating Life (Self-Talk):** While historically associated with "losing your mind," talking to yourself is incredibly common and actually a sign of high cognitive function. People will narrate their actions ("Okay, first I'll grab the keys, then I need to find my wallet...") to help organize their thoughts and focus.
* **Subconscious Mouth Movements:** Have you ever watched someone concentrate really hard—like threading a needle, drawing, or playing a video game—and noticed their tongue sticking out? Or perhaps they mimic the motion of scissors with their mouth while cutting paper. 
* **The "Imaginary Interview":** Many people construct elaborate interviews or debates in their head while showering or driving. They will literally explain their life choices, hobbies, or political views to an imaginary talk-show host or a phantom podcast audience.

### 4. Digital & Domestic Oddities
Modern life has birthed entirely new categories of strange behaviors.
* **The "Clear All" Obsession:** Many people cannot tolerate notification badges on their smartphones. They will open apps they don't care about just to make the little red "1" disappear, or constantly swipe away background apps even though modern operating systems don't require it.
* **Volume Number Rules:** When adjusting the volume on a TV or car radio, some people *must* set it to an even number, or a multiple of five. Leaving the volume on an odd number like 13 or 17 can cause genuine, mild distress.
* **The "Fake Scroll":** When walking past someone on the street or waiting in an awkward social situation, people will pull out their phones and intensely scroll through their home screens, pretending to read something incredibly important when they are actually just swiping past blank apps.

Do you recognize any of these habits in yourself, or do you have a unique quirk of your own?
